content: Flaxseed should be dosed according to specific indications. For oral administration, the recommended dosage is 1 tablespoon taken two to three times daily (BID-TID), or 15-50 grams per day. Alternatively, 15-30 milliliters can be taken orally once daily, which is equivalent to 200 milligrams of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) per day. For topical use, 30-50 grams can be applied as needed (PRN). It is essential to consume flaxseed with an adequate amount of fluid to prevent bowel obstruction. Flaxseed may be used for various conditions, including chronic constipation, benign prostatic hyperplasia (when using flaxseed oil), cancer prevention, diabetes, diverticulitis, gastritis or enteritis, hypercholesterolemia, irritable bowel syndrome, menopausal symptoms, myocardial infarction prevention (when using flaxseed oil), skin inflammation, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) nephritis. It is possibly effective for managing diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, menopausal symptoms, and SLE nephritis. Flaxseed contains phytoestrogens, which may interact with other substances through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially increasing their effects. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is recommended when using flaxseed in combination with other phytoestrogen-containing substances. Adverse effects associated with flaxseed include allergic reactions, anaphylactoid reactions, diarrhea (particularly with flaxseed oil), and intestinal obstruction. Conditions such as bowel obstruction, breast, ovarian, or uterine cancer, endometriosis, esophageal strictures, hormone-sensitive conditions, hypertriglyceridemia, acute intestinal inflammation, and uterine fibroids may contraindicate its use. Flaxseed oil may also pose risks for individuals with bleeding disorders. The safety of flaxseed during pregnancy and lactation has not been extensively studied. It is recommended to consult a healthcare professional before use. Moderate consumption is believed to be beneficial, and the nutrients in flaxseed may support breast milk production. In general, flaxseed is considered acceptable for use during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
